strengths: The paper proposes a clear and interesting statistical model for image classification in which within-class variability comes from geometric deformations of latent template images rather than additive label/input noise. This is a useful perspective and is well motivated by the limitations of treating pixels as unrelated high-dimensional covariates.

The alignment/nearest-neighbor results in Section 3 are conceptually appealing: under explicit separation conditions, the paper shows perfect classification with very few samples, and the lower-bound construction explains why a separation rate of order 1/d is unavoidable under Lipschitz regularity.

The manuscript is mathematically ambitious and mostly well organized. It connects deformation models, invariance, nearest-neighbor classification, and CNN expressivity/generalization in a coherent narrative, with concrete examples such as affine, scale/shift, rotation, and wave-like deformations.

The limitations and extensions discussion is honest about important missing pieces: background noise, multiple objects, partial visibility, perspective transformations, richer deformation classes, and the fact that the model is a prototype rather than a realistic full image model.
weaknesses: A central technical issue appears in the CNN learning formulation. Equation (27), described as empirical misclassification error, minimizes -1/n sum_i k_i 1(q2(X_i)>1/2). This objective rewards predicting class 1 on positive examples but does not penalize false positives on class-0 examples, and is not equivalent to 0-1 empirical risk. The later equivalence in Eq. (94) to minimizing classification error is therefore false as written, which undermines Theorem 4.1 and the claimed CNN misclassification bound.

The strongest CNN claims rely on an idealized ERM over 0-1 loss and a specially constructed architecture, while the experiments train standard Keras CNNs with Adam/cross-entropy-like practice. The manuscript only conjectures extension to surrogate losses, so the empirical CNN results do not directly validate the stated theorem.

The deformation model is highly idealized: binary classification, nonnegative zero-background images, fully visible single objects, no additive/background noise in the main theory, known deformation class, and strong separation assumptions. These assumptions are useful for analysis but substantially limit significance for practical image classification.

The empirical study is too small to support broad claims. It uses synthetic augmentations of selected MNIST templates, N=100 test samples, 30 repetitions, only median errors, limited architecture tuning, and no confidence intervals or detailed deformation parameter ranges. The experiments mainly confirm that a hand-matched alignment classifier works well under its own generative assumptions.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper specifies Keras ImageDataGenerator and broad CNN architectures but does not provide code, seeds, exact augmentation ranges, optimizer/training schedules beyond the default learning rate, epoch counts, stopping criteria, selected templates, or raw numerical tables underlying Figure 8.

There are presentation and notation issues that make verification harder: some theorem statements use ambiguous rendered notation such as D > sqrt(kappa/d), Eq. (31) switches from pixel averages to point evaluations, Theorem 4.2 defines the classifier using bp2 rather than the displayed oracle network component, and several constants/assumptions are buried in long appendices.

strengths: The paper tackles an important theoretical gap: image classification models often treat pixels as high-dimensional covariates, while many real image variations are structured deformations of underlying objects.
The proposed deformation-based statistical framework is conceptually useful and includes shifts, scaling, brightness changes, rotations, affine transformations, and some nonlinear deformations.
The image-alignment/nearest-neighbor benchmark is cleanly motivated, and the perfect-classification result under a separation condition gives a useful reference point for this stylized setting.
The paper attempts a nontrivial CNN analysis, including an explicit architecture, approximation argument, and VC-style generalization bound, rather than only giving informal intuition.
The manuscript is mathematically substantial and includes detailed appendices, plus a lower-bound discussion indicating that the separation rate is not merely an artifact of the upper-bound proof.
weaknesses: A central technical definition appears incorrect: Eq. (27) is described as empirical misclassification error, but the displayed objective minimizes only a negative reward for predicting class 1 on positive samples, with no penalty for false positives. This would favor trivial all-positive predictions and does not match the VC oracle inequality later used in the proof of Theorem 4.1. As written, this undermines the main CNN theorem.

The theoretical setting is highly idealized: deterministic labels, no additive noise, zero/fully removable background, fully visible objects, known deformation class, brightness removable by normalization, and strong separation between class templates. These assumptions make the conclusions much less informative for realistic image classification than the introduction suggests.

The CNN contribution is weaker than advertised. The analyzed classifier is an exact 0-1 ERM over a specially constructed CNN class, while the experiments train ordinary CNNs with Adam/Keras. The paper does not bridge this gap, so the empirical section does not really validate the theorem.

The empirical study is very small and synthetic: it uses deformations of one or a few MNIST templates, sample sizes up to 64, only N=100 test examples, and reports medians over 30 repetitions without uncertainty intervals or implementation details sufficient to assess robustness.

The main CNN bound scales as |A_d|^2/n up to logs, and |A_d| can grow polynomially in image resolution. For the discussed deformation classes this can be very large, but the paper does not convincingly explain practical regimes where the result is meaningful.

Several claims are overstated. The paper suggests a refined understanding of CNN image classification, overparameterization, and data augmentation, but the analysis mostly shows that a hand-designed convolutional architecture can separate two template classes under strong deformation and separation assumptions.

Presentation has important precision problems beyond Eq. (27), including notation inconsistencies around constructed versus learned classifiers in Theorem 4.2 and its proof, and occasional broad prose that obscures the gap between the stylized model and real image recognition.

Reproducibility is limited. The numerical section gives high-level Keras/ImageDataGenerator and architecture descriptions, but lacks seeds, exact augmentation ranges, code, template IDs, optimizer/training schedules beyond the default learning rate, and sufficient details for reproducing Figure 8.

The paper contains no substantive research-ethics or limitations discussion beyond future-extension remarks. The limitations are central to interpreting the work and should be explicitly separated and discussed.

Originality is moderate rather than high: deformation/template models, image alignment, invariant classifiers, and CNN invariance analyses are established themes. The paper’s value is in a specific statistical formalization, but the current technical and evidential weaknesses prevent acceptance.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and original statistical model for image classification in which intra-class variation comes from geometric deformations of latent template images rather than additive noise. This is a useful perspective that helps explain why increasing image resolution can make classification easier under the model, contrasting with standard high-dimensional nonparametric classification intuitions.

The theoretical development is substantial: the paper gives exact-classification results for deformation-aware nearest-neighbor/alignment classifiers, verifies assumptions for affine, rotation/scale/shift, wave-like, and composed deformation classes, and provides a matching lower-bound argument showing the 1/d separation rate is necessary for the alignment setting.

The CNN analysis is conceptually interesting. The construction links convolutional filters and global max-pooling to invariance over discretized deformation classes, yielding a misclassification bound depending on the deformation-class complexity rather than directly suffering a full pixel-dimensional curse.

The exposition is mostly self-contained and readable for a theory paper. The authors are transparent that the first inverse-mapping classifier is mainly a theoretical benchmark, that the alignment classifier relies on a special deformation model, and that background noise, partial visibility, perspective transformations, blur, and richer registration models remain important extensions.

The MNIST-derived experiments are small but well aligned with the theory: they compare an image-alignment classifier and CNNs in low-sample regimes under controlled random deformations, and they illustrate the advantage of explicitly exploiting the deformation structure.
weaknesses: There is a serious soundness issue in the CNN section as written. Equation (27) defines the empirical objective as minimizing -1/n sum_i k_i 1(q_2(X_i)>1/2), which is not the empirical misclassification error and would encourage predicting class 1 on positive examples without penalizing false positives. The later claimed equivalence in equation (94) to 0-1 ERM is false for this objective. This may be a typo, but it is central to Theorem 4.1's proof and should be corrected and checked throughout.

The theoretical guarantees rely on restrictive assumptions: zero background for the main alignment classifier, full visibility of objects, nonnegative templates, Lipschitz templates with compact support, known deformation class, and separation conditions over all allowed deformations. These are reasonable for a prototype model, but they limit the direct applicability to natural images where clutter, occlusion, multiple objects, blur, and nuisance variation beyond the modeled deformation class are common.

The CNN result is existential and tied to a specially constructed architecture and exact 0-1 empirical risk minimization, which the paper itself notes is computationally intractable. The connection to practical CNN training with cross-entropy and SGD/Adam is only conjectural, while the empirical CNNs used in Section 5 are standard Keras architectures rather than the theoretically analyzed architecture.

The empirical section is too limited to fully support the broader claims about CNNs and deformation invariance. It uses MNIST-derived binary tasks, small test sets of N=100, median over 30 repetitions, and only a few sample sizes. Details such as random deformation ranges, preprocessing thresholds for support detection, seeds, code availability, and uncertainty intervals are not sufficiently specified for reproducibility.

The paper discusses limitations and future extensions honestly, but reproducibility is only moderate: proofs are included, yet the experimental protocol lacks enough implementation detail, and there is no apparent code or data-generation script release. Research ethics concerns appear minimal because the experiments use MNIST-like digit data, but the paper does not include a dedicated ethics or broader impacts discussion.

strengths: The manuscript proposes a clear and useful deformation-based statistical model for image classification, contrasting with pixel-wise nonparametric denoising views and formalizing variability from shifts, scaling, brightness, rotations, and some nonlinear deformations.

The theoretical development is substantial: the inverse-mapping and alignment classifiers have perfect-classification guarantees under explicit separation conditions, and Theorem 3.8 gives a matching lower-bound intuition showing why a 1/d separation scale is necessary under the pixelized model.

The CNN analysis is a meaningful contribution: it connects a concrete one-convolution-layer/global-pooling architecture to deformation invariance and derives misclassification bounds for both 0-1 ERM and cross-entropy ERM, with dependence on the deformation covering complexity.

The paper is generally well organized and mathematically detailed, with extensive appendices proving the main results and a helpful discussion relating the framework to registration, functional data analysis, scattering transforms, and invariant representations.
The limitations section is honest about important gaps such as background noise, multiple objects, occlusion, sharp edges, perspective transforms, and more realistic deformation models.
weaknesses: The practical relevance is limited by very strong modeling assumptions: zero or simple background, fully visible single objects, nonnegative template functions, deterministic labels, known deformation class, strong separation between template orbits, and often global ERM over a prescribed CNN class. These assumptions are far from typical natural-image classification.

The empirical study is weak relative to the scope of the claims. Training and test data are synthetically generated from one or a few fixed templates using the same deformation process assumed by the theory, so the experiments mostly verify the model construction rather than demonstrating usefulness on real classification distributions.

There are no comparisons to standard baselines such as ordinary k-NN, data-augmented CNNs, spatial transformer networks, group-equivariant CNNs, scattering classifiers, or registration-based baselines on the same synthetic tasks. This makes it hard to judge whether the proposed classifiers or theory explain anything beyond a controlled toy regime.

The CNN theory and experiments are not tightly matched. The approximation results rely on filters constructed from the unknown template functions and deformation cover, while the experiments train small conventional Keras CNNs with Adam and fixed filter sizes. The manuscript does not quantify how the implemented architectures correspond to the theoretical covering sizes or block-structured filters.

The paper claims that increasing image resolution makes the problem easier in the deformation model, but the CNN bound in Theorem 4.1 grows with d through the architecture/covering complexity, and the discussion only partially reconciles this. A sharper explanation of regimes where resolution helps versus hurts would strengthen the contribution.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript gives datasets, rough architectures, optimizer, sample sizes, and repetitions, but no code link, random seeds, exact deformation parameter distributions/ranges, preprocessing details for CIFAR/ImageNet backgrounds, or hardware/training details.

The treatment of ethics and broader impacts is essentially absent. The work is mostly theoretical and low-risk, but it uses image datasets and discusses object recognition; at least a brief statement on dataset provenance, licenses, and possible misuse or bias would be appropriate.

Presentation is mostly clear but lengthy and sometimes oversells the generality. The title is vague, several claims about image-classification variability are broader than the evidence supports, and the main experimental figures are summarized qualitatively without enough numerical detail or uncertainty beyond medians.

strengths: The manuscript addresses a meaningful theoretical gap: image-classification theory often treats pixels as high-dimensional covariates with additive/noisy labels, while this paper instead models within-class variation as geometric deformations of latent template functions. This is a reasonable and potentially useful abstraction for understanding invariance.

The paper provides nontrivial formal results. The inverse-mapping and alignment classifiers are analyzed under explicit separation conditions, including a necessity-style result for the 1/d separation scale, and the CNN section derives misclassification bounds for ERM under 0-1 and cross-entropy losses.

The CNN construction makes a clear attempt to connect architectural features, especially convolution plus global max-pooling, to invariance under shifts and approximation over discretized deformation classes. This is more targeted than generic norm-based generalization bounds.

The presentation is generally coherent for a theory paper: assumptions are stated, proofs are extensive, and the paper includes discussion of related work in functional data analysis, scattering transforms, registration, and invariant representations.
weaknesses: The contribution is much less convincing as an ICML main-track paper because the central model is highly idealized. Images are assumed to be generated from one template per class through controlled deformations, often with black/zero background and full visibility. This excludes many core difficulties of modern image classification, including intra-class semantic diversity, clutter, texture/background correlations, occlusion, multiple objects, label ambiguity, and nuisance variation not representable by the deformation class.

The theoretical guarantees rely on strong and sometimes impractical knowledge. The inverse-mapping classifier requires knowledge/discretization of the deformation class and essentially searches over transformations; the alignment classifier depends on support-based normalization that is fragile to background, noise, and partial visibility; the CNN bounds require a designed architecture tied to a covering of the deformation class and analyze ERM rather than the actual trained optimizer.

The CNN results have limited explanatory force for practical CNNs. The analyzed architecture uses one convolutional layer, global max-pooling, bounded parameters, normalized grayscale-style inputs, and filters constructed to match deformed templates. This is far from modern CNN/Vision architectures and does not explain feature learning in realistic settings. The paper also explicitly acknowledges that the training routine is excluded from the statistical analysis.

The empirical study is weak and largely circular relative to the theory. The experiments generate synthetic samples by deforming a single selected template image per class from MNIST/FashionMNIST/CIFAR/ImageNet, so they mostly test whether methods work under the assumed data-generating process. This does not establish relevance to real classification datasets with natural within-class variability.

Baselines are inadequate. The numerical section compares only the proposed inverse mapping, alignment, and small CNN variants, without standard baselines such as nearest neighbors on raw pixels/features, data-augmented CNNs, spatial transformer networks, group-equivariant CNNs, scattering features, registration-based classifiers, or modern pretrained features. As a result, the empirical claims about usefulness are not well supported.

The paper overstates practical significance. Statements that the framework may explain near-perfect classification or data augmentation are not backed by experiments or theory in realistic regimes. The results mostly show that classification is possible when class identity is exactly preserved under a known deformation model and the template classes are sufficiently separated.

Reproducibility is only partial. The mathematical statements are detailed, but the experiments lack important implementation details: exact selected template images, deformation parameter distributions/ranges, preprocessing choices, random seeds, number of epochs, batch size, optimizer settings beyond Adam learning rate, stopping criteria, and code availability. Median-over-10 with small test sets is also too limited for reliable empirical conclusions.

The paper is very long and not well calibrated for the venue. Much of the 81-page manuscript is proof material, while the main paper does not sufficiently distill the conceptual contribution, compare against the closest modern ML methods, or clarify which assumptions are essential versus technical.

Limitations are mentioned in the conclusion, including structured backgrounds, noise, occlusion, sharp edges, and perspective transformations, but these limitations are fundamental to the applicability of the framework rather than minor extensions. The paper does not empirically stress-test these failure modes.

Ethical risks are not a central issue here, but the manuscript also lacks a standard broader-impact or dataset-use discussion. More importantly, because experiments use public image datasets only as sources of templates for synthetic generation, the empirical conclusions should be framed much more narrowly.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful shift in statistical modeling for image classification: variability is modeled as geometric deformation of class templates rather than additive noise in a high-dimensional covariate space. This is a meaningful conceptual contribution for understanding why image resolution and invariance can help rather than hurt.

The theoretical development is substantial. The inverse-mapping and image-alignment classifiers obtain exact recovery under an explicit separation condition, and the paper also gives a non-identifiability lower-bound argument showing the 1/d separation scale is not merely an artifact of the analysis.

The CNN analysis is one of the strongest parts: the authors explicitly connect deformation covering complexity, image resolution, network size, and sample size, and provide rates for both 0-1 ERM and cross-entropy ERM. The constructive approximation argument makes the result more informative than a generic generalization bound.

The manuscript is generally well organized and careful about positioning relative to image registration, functional data analysis, scattering transforms, and existing neural-network theory. It also acknowledges important limitations around optimization, complex backgrounds, occlusions, and richer deformation models.

The empirical section, while limited, is aligned with the theory: synthetic deformations from MNIST/FashionMNIST/CIFAR/ImageNet templates show the predicted trends that alignment methods can recover labels with very small class coverage and that larger CNN architectures perform better under richer deformation sets.
weaknesses: The statistical model is quite stylized relative to natural image classification. The main guarantees rely on fixed class templates, fully visible objects, controlled deformation classes, nonnegative intensities, binary classification, and strong separation. These assumptions are mathematically clean but limit the direct practical significance of the claims.

The CNN results are for idealized empirical risk minimizers rather than the actual training algorithm. The paper discusses this honestly, but it remains a material gap because the empirical section uses Adam-trained Keras CNNs while the theorems do not establish that such training finds the required classifier.

The empirical evidence is modest for an ICML main-track claim. The experiments use one or a few templates per class with synthetically generated deformations, small test sizes, and median over 10 repetitions. There is no comparison to standard CNNs trained with conventional augmentation, spatial transformer networks, scattering features, registration baselines, or modern invariant/equivariant architectures.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone. The experiments mention Keras ImageDataGenerator and default Adam settings, but do not specify all transformation ranges, preprocessing details, seeds, code availability, exact train/test generation protocol, or confidence intervals. This would make it hard to independently reproduce the figures precisely.

Some separation quantities and constants are hard to interpret operationally. The results are theoretically valid under the stated conditions, but the paper does not give enough diagnostics showing that the assumptions or separation thresholds hold for the empirical templates, so the experiments mainly illustrate rather than validate the theory.

Presentation is strong overall, but the main paper is long and technically dense. Some claims about relevance to real-world images and overparameterization would benefit from more cautious wording or more direct empirical support. Ethical impacts are not discussed explicitly, though no major unresolved ethical concern is apparent for this theoretical work.
